name: Thermo-Calc Software AB
subcategory: closed CALPHAD computational thermodynamics and kinetics (Thermo-Calc, DICTRA, TC-PRISMA, AM Module, databases)
origin_detail: Development began in 1977 in Mats Hillert's physical metallurgy department at KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm. Three of his graduate students, Bo Sundman, Bo Jansson and John Ågren, started the work, and the first version was completed in 1981. In 1993 the seven researchers who had built it donated their individual rights to a foundation, Stiftelsen för Tillämpad Termodynamik (STT), to keep the IP in one entity. Thermo-Calc Software AB was formed in 1997 because commercial activity did not fit the institute's academic mission. STT remains the majority owner. HQ in Solna (Stockholm), with subsidiaries in the USA (McMurray, PA), Korea, Brazil, China and India.
openness_notes: Proprietary software and databases sold as licences. The AM Module needs a Thermo-Calc licence, a module licence and a supported database. Programmatic access is through proprietary SDKs (TC-Python, TC-Toolbox for MATLAB, TQ-Interface), which are interfaces to closed code, not open source. No terms were found for the 1981-1997 academic distribution from KTH, so openness_initial = 0 rests on the absence of any public source release. The TDB database file format it popularised is the main open interface: the open pycalphad reads 'Thermo-Calc TDB' files.

license_history.license: Proprietary (commercial licences plus maintenance and support subscriptions)
license_history.note: Company formed in 1997 to carry the commercial activity; maintenance-and-support subscribers were surveyed in 2025.

risk_events: 1993: IP consolidated in the STT foundation after the seven developers donated their individual rights, the founding governance fix for multi-author academic code
1997: commercialised as a company because commercial activity did not fit KTH's academic mission
2025: launched Thermo-Calc Solutions, an engineering-services division, diversifying beyond licences
2025 customer survey: 21% of respondents already used an LLM or AI assistant for Thermo-Calc work, and the company says it is 'exploring how to integrate ML and AI tools into our CALPHAD framework'

Open alternatives read its file format: pycalphad (MIT) and OpenCalphad (GPL inferred). OpenCalphad's first version was co-written by a Bo Sundman, the name of one of Thermo-Calc's three original developers
robustness: Nearly 50 years of continuous development. A foundation (STT) is the majority owner rather than VC or PE. 2,000+ customer organisations in 60+ countries, 50,000+ journal citations, and twice-yearly releases (2026a, 2026b). Users cannot fork or audit the code or the commercial databases, so continuity depends on one firm. The open TDB format and the open CALPHAD codes are partial hedges.
physical_science_relevance: Thermo-Calc is the default CALPHAD tool for alloy design in metallurgy, the Digital Alloy Lab's field. Its Additive Manufacturing Module (2023) models powder-bed fusion with a laser or electron-beam heat source (Gaussian, core-ring or top-hat): melt-pool behaviour, solidification and evaporation-driven composition change across tracks and layers. It produces printability maps for keyholing, lack of fusion and balling, with alloy properties from an extended Scheil calculator, and it couples to DICTRA, TC-PRISMA and a CET model for microstructure. An Al database is among those the AM module supports. TC-Python exposes most AM-module functions, so it can be scripted inside high-throughput or self-driving alloy-design loops for LPBF aluminium alloys. Every node in such a loop needs a paid licence, though, and results rest on closed databases.
openness_effect_assessment: Thermo-Calc is a closed academic spin-off that has lasted. The code moved from a KTH research group into a foundation-owned company and stayed closed, funded by licences and maintenance, and it became the reference CALPHAD tool (50,000+ citations, 2,000+ customer organisations). Staying closed did not stop open alternatives: pycalphad and OpenCalphad do the core equilibrium calculations and read the TDB format. Our assessment is that the vendor's moat is its assessed databases and integrated kinetics and AM modules, which the open projects found here do not offer.
key_takeaway: Thermo-Calc is the closed incumbent that defines the CALPHAD workflow an LPBF alloy lab uses. A KTH research code became a foundation-owned company in 1997, and it sells licences, databases and now services, with a scriptable but proprietary Python API. Its longevity (development since 1977) and steady releases show that a closed academic spin-off can be durable without venture capital. For a lab that wants to work openly, the practical split is to use Thermo-Calc for the commercial databases and the AM module, and to publish assessments as TDB files and workflows in pycalphad, so others can reproduce the work without a licence.
funding_sources: Project funding such as Sweden's WISE programme (Li-ion batteries, Nov 2025; amount not given)
